A bobbin is a small spool — a cylindrical object with wider rims on each end — around which thread, yarn, or wire is wound for storage and controlled release.

Think of it like a tiny version of the large rolls of thread you see in shops. The difference is that a bobbin is compact, precisely shaped, and designed to work inside a machine or a craft setup — not just sit on a shelf.

Picture a capsule or a short cylinder. It has:

  • A central barrel (the tube part), around which the material is wound.
  • Two flat disc-like ends (called flanges), which stick out slightly wider than the barrel, keeping the wound material from sliding off the sides.

The whole thing is usually very small — often fitting between your thumb and forefinger — though size varies depending on where it's used. It can be made of plastic, metal, wood, or even bone (in traditional crafts).

The word "bobbin" appears in several different fields, and the concept is the same across all of them: a spool that holds and releases thread, yarn, or wire in a controlled, tidy way.

1. Sewing Machines (the most common use)

This is where most people first encounter the word.

A sewing machine works by interlocking two separate threads to form a stitch — one thread comes from above (from the large spool sitting on top of the machine), and one comes from below. The thread below is held on a bobbin.

The bobbin is loaded into a small compartment underneath the needle plate (the flat metal surface you sew over). As the machine runs, the needle pulls the top thread down, loops it around the bobbin thread underneath, and the two lock together to form a stitch. Without the bobbin providing that lower thread, the machine simply cannot sew.

Before you start sewing, you have to:

  • Wind your thread onto the bobbin (most machines help you do this automatically).
  • Insert the bobbin correctly into its compartment.

When the bobbin runs out of thread, your stitches start failing — a familiar frustration for anyone who sews.

2. Lace-Making (traditional craft)

Bobbin lace is a centuries-old craft where intricate, delicate lace is made entirely by hand using many bobbins at once — sometimes dozens or even hundreds for a single piece of lace.

In this context, each bobbin is a small, often decorative wooden or bone object with thread wound around its lower half. The lace-maker works on a padded pillow with pins stuck into a pattern. The bobbins hang down from the pins, and the maker weaves, crosses, and twists them over and under each other according to the pattern. Each bobbin feeds out its thread as the work progresses.

The bobbins serve two purposes here: they store the thread and act as weights to keep tension in the threads, preventing them from going limp or tangled.

3. Textile Mills and Spinning (industrial)

In factories that spin and weave fabric, bobbins (sometimes larger ones, also called spools or cops depending on shape) are used throughout the process. Yarn is wound onto bobbins at the spinning stage, then transferred between machines as the yarn gets processed, twisted, dyed, or woven into cloth.

In this setting, bobbins are workhorses — they're constantly filled, emptied, and refilled as thread moves through different stages of production.

4. Electronics and Electrical Engineering

In this context, a bobbin is a spool-shaped frame (usually plastic) around which thin copper wire is wound many times to create a coil. This wound bobbin is then used in components like:

  • Transformers (which change voltage levels in electrical circuits)
  • Inductors (which store energy in a magnetic field)

Here, the bobbin isn't just a storage device — it's a structural part of the component itself. It holds the wire windings in precise shape and insulates them from the metal core running through the centre.
The Unifying Idea Across All Uses

No matter where you see the word, a bobbin always does the same fundamental thing: it organises and controls the release of a long, continuous material (thread, yarn, wire) by keeping it neatly wound on a compact, handy spool. Without it, you'd have a tangled, unusable mess.

• "She ran out of thread on her bobbin mid-seam and had to stop to refill it."
  • "The lace-maker's pillow was covered with over sixty bobbins, each one carrying a different thread."
  • "The transformer's bobbin was wound with hundreds of turns of fine copper wire."

A bobbin is a small spool with raised ends, used to hold and smoothly release thread, yarn, or wire — most famously found inside a sewing machine as the source of the lower thread that forms a stitch.
